name: ICL7660AIBAZA-T
title: ICL7660S, ICL7660A: CMOS charge-pump voltage converters, 1.5 V to 12 V
summary: The ICL7660S and ICL7660A are switched-capacitor converters in CMOS that turn a positive supply of 1.5 V to 12 V into a negative output close to -V+, using only an external pump capacitor and an output reservoir capacitor. Inside are a series supply regulator, an RC oscillator that free-runs near 10 kHz at 5 V, a level translator and four MOS power switches, with logic that keeps the output-switch substrates biased against latch-up. The same chip can double a positive voltage, split a supply in half, be cascaded or paralleled, and be run from an external clock. The ICL7660S adds a BOOST pin that raises the oscillator about 3.5 times; on the ICL7660A that pin has no connection. The ICL7660AIBAZA-T is the ICL7660A in a lead-free 8-lead narrow SOIC for -40 °C to +85 °C, on tape and reel.

circuits.title: ICL7660S test circuit
circuits.description: The ICL7660S is measured as an inverter from a +5 V supply. C1 is the pump capacitor across CAP+ and CAP-, C2 the reservoir from VOUT to ground, and RL the load, wired from V+ to the negative output so the supply current IS covers the load current IL. One switch takes BOOST to V+ for the boosted-frequency tests and another takes LV to ground for the low-voltage tests. OSC has nothing on it. A Schottky diode, anode at VOUT and cathode at CAP-, may be added.

circuits.title: ICL7660A test circuit
circuits.description: The ICL7660A is measured the same way as the ICL7660S: 10 µF pump and reservoir capacitors, a load RL from V+ to the negative output, and a switch from LV to ground. Pin 1 has no connection. A capacitor COSC from OSC to ground may be fitted to lower the oscillator frequency.

circuits.title: Simple negative voltage converter
circuits.description: The basic inverter: a positive supply of +1.5 V to +12 V on V+ gives an output near -V+. C1 is the pump capacitor between CAP+ and CAP-, C2 the reservoir on the output with its positive end grounded. LV goes to ground only when the supply is below 3.5 V. The Schottky diode (anode VOUT, cathode CAP-) is fitted where the latch-up conditions of the design rules call for it. Seen from the load, the output behaves as a source of -(V+) behind a series resistance RO.

parts.note: fitted only for a supply below 3.5V

notes: Pin 1 is BOOST on the ICL7660S and NC on the ICL7660A; it is left open.

circuits.title: External clocking
circuits.description: A CMOS gate powered from the same V+ drives OSC through a 1 kΩ series resistor, which is required to keep the converter out of latch-up. The pump runs at half the clock frequency and the output switches on the clock's rising edge. The rest is the basic inverter with 10 µF pump and reservoir capacitors. A clock made with TTL logic also needs a 10 kΩ pull-up to V+.

circuits.title: Lowering the oscillator frequency
circuits.description: A capacitor COSC from OSC to V+ slows the oscillator, which cuts switching losses and raises efficiency at light load. C1 and C2 are raised by the same factor as the frequency falls: 100 pF brings the oscillator from 10 kHz to 1 kHz, and C1 and C2 then go from 10 µF to 100 µF.

circuits.title: Positive voltage doubler
circuits.description: VOUT is grounded and CAP+ drives the low end of C1. While CAP+ is low, D1 charges C1 from V+ to V+ - VF; when CAP+ swings up to V+, the stacked voltage passes through D2 onto C2. The output is (2V+) - (2VF), about 60 Ω source impedance at V+ = 5 V and 10 mA. D1 and D2 may be any suitable diode.

circuits.title: Combined negative converter and positive doubler
circuits.description: One converter gives both -V+ and about 2V+, for instance -5 V and +9 V from +5 V. C1 pumps and C3 holds the negative output; C2 pumps and C4 holds the doubled output through D1 and D2. Both outputs are driven from CAP+, so each has a higher source impedance than when built alone. An optional Schottky D3 goes anode to VOUT, cathode to CAP-.

circuits.title: Splitting a supply in half
circuits.description: Run backwards, the converter holds its GND pin midway between a supply V+ and V-, giving VOUT = (V+ - V-)/2 at the centre node. The switches carry the load in parallel, so the output impedance is lower and more current is available than from the inverting circuits. Two 50 µF capacitors hold the halves and a third is the pump; RL1 and RL2 are the loads on each half. LV is wired to the centre node. A high-value resistor to LV ensures start-up. +15 V split this way and then inverted gives a nominal -15 V with about 250 Ω series output resistance.

circuits.title: Regulating the output voltage
circuits.description: An ICL7611 op amp sets the converter's supply so the negative output stays nearly constant as the load changes. An ICL8069 reference, fed from +8 V through 56k, drives both op-amp inputs through 50k and 100k. The output returns to the non-inverting input through 800k and a 250k adjustment pot. The inverting input has 50k to a node held by 100 Ω to ground and coupled by 10 µF to the op-amp output, which supplies V+ of the converter. This delays the loop enough for the converter's switching lag; feedback taken straight to the output is not used. With 100 µF pump and output capacitors the output impedance is under 5 Ω at 10 mA.

operation.text: Each device holds a series DC supply regulator, an RC oscillator with a divide-by-two counter, a voltage level translator, four MOS output switches and a substrate logic network. Unloaded at 5 V the oscillator runs near 10 kHz; a capacitor on OSC slows it and an external clock can override it.

On one half-cycle S1 and S3 close and charge C1 to V+; on the other, S2 and S4 close and lay C1 across C2, so with ideal switches and no load C2 sits at exactly -V+. S1 is a P-channel MOSFET and S2, S3, S4 are N-channel. Only C1 and C2 are external, and they can be inexpensive 10 µF polarised electrolytics.

The substrates of S3 and S4 must stay reverse biased to their sources without degrading their on-resistance. At start-up and with the output shorted (VOUT = V+) the substrate logic senses VOUT and, with the level translators, switches those substrates to the right level; without this the part would burn power and probably latch up. Both parts run with no external diode across the whole temperature and voltage range.

operation.topic: LV pin and the internal regulator
operation.text: The regulator is part of the anti-latch-up circuit, but its drop hurts operation at low supply. Tying LV to GND switches it out and improves low-voltage operation (1.5 V to 3.5 V). Above 3.5 V, LV must be left open to keep the part latch-up proof and undamaged. Current into LV is limited to 20 µA above 3.5 V.

A converter approaches 100 % efficiency when its drive circuit draws little, its switches have very low on-resistance and no offset, and the capacitors' impedance is negligible at the pump frequency. With large C1 and C2 these parts come close. C2 is made large to cut ripple and C1 large to keep efficiency up. Power efficiency is 98 % typ (96 % min) at RL = 5 kΩ and voltage conversion efficiency 99.9 % typ unloaded.

Stay within the maximum supply voltage. Do not tie LV to GND above 3.5 V. Above 5.5 V, do not hold the output shorted to V+ for long; brief conditions, start-up included, are acceptable. With polarised capacitors, C1's + goes to pin 2 and C2's + goes to GND. A supply with 25 Ω to 30 Ω source impedance may need 2.2 µF from pin 8 to ground to hold the input slew under 2 V/µs. Above 5 V input with a rise faster than 2 V/µs, a Schottky diode with its anode on VOUT and cathode on CAP- keeps pin 5 from going above pin 4 and so stops latch-up through Q4's body diode. Pin 5 must never go above GND (pin 3); where the load can pull VOUT up before the IC is running, a 1N914 or similar diode across C2 (anode pin 5, cathode pin 3) prevents latch-up.

No pin may go above V+ or below GND. Signals from separately powered sources should not reach LV or OSC before the converter itself has power. Below 5.5 V supply, LV and OSC may range from -0.3 V to V+ + 0.3 V; above 5.5 V, from V+ - 5.5 V to V+ + 0.3 V.

The output behaves as -(V+) behind a resistance RO set by the switch on-resistance, the pump frequency, C1, C2 and the ESR of both capacitors. Bigger capacitors shrink the 1/(fPUMP × C1) term and low-ESR capacitors shrink the ESR terms. Raising the oscillator frequency shrinks 1/(fPUMP × C1), but with C1 above 10 µF the shorter cycle may not fully charge the capacitors and RO can rise overall. Low ESR in C2 also lowers output ripple.

On the ICL7660S, BOOST (pin 1) tied to V+ raises the oscillator charge and discharge current and lifts the frequency about 3.5 times, lowering output impedance and ripple. This lets small capacitors such as 0.1 µF reach output currents similar to the free-running part with 10 µF or 100 µF (Figure 11), which suits surface-mount designs. An external clock on OSC also raises the frequency; it must drive through a 1 kΩ series resistor, a TTL clock also needs a 10 kΩ pull-up to V+, the pump runs at half the clock frequency, and the output switches on the clock's rising edge.

A capacitor on OSC slows the oscillator, cutting switching loss and raising efficiency at light load. The pump and reservoir capacitors' impedance rises in step, so C1 and C2 are scaled up by the same factor: 100 pF lowers 10 kHz to 1 kHz, with C1 and C2 raised from 10 µF to 100 µF. The frequency may also be changed for reasons of noise, among others. In the test circuits, COSC above 1000 pF calls for C1 and C2 of 100 µF.
Wired as a doubler the part reaches up to 22.8 V from a 12 V input. In the two-diode doubler the output source impedance is about 60 Ω at V+ = 5 V and 10 mA.

Any number of devices may share one reservoir capacitor, each with its own pump capacitor, dividing the output resistance by the number of devices. Devices may be cascaded for larger negative multiples of the supply; finite efficiency limits this to about ten devices at light load.

Where the load current swings widely, the converter's output impedance can be a problem. Controlling its supply with a low-power op amp holds the output nearly constant. Feedback taken directly from the output is not used because the output follows an input change only once the switching delay has passed; the loop in Figure 21 is slowed to suit. Larger pump and storage capacitors help, and the values given reach under 5 Ω output impedance at 10 mA.
Thermal resistance θJA is 110 °C/W for the PDIP and 160 °C/W for the SOIC (θJC 59 and 48 °C/W). Power is derated linearly by 5.5 mW/°C above 50 °C.
